name: Iselin disease
aliases: traction apophysitis of the fifth metatarsal
osteochondrosis of the fifth metatarsal base

reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A traction apophysitis at the base of the fifth metatarsal rather than a true osteonecrosis
Affected site is the apophysis at the base of the fifth metatarsal, at the insertion of the peroneus brevis tendon
Typically affects active children, roughly eight to thirteen years of age around the time the apophysis appears
Presents with pain, tenderness and sometimes swelling over the lateral border of the midfoot, aggravated by running and cutting or inversion activities
The radiographic hallmark is an enlarged or fragmented apophysis at the fifth metatarsal base oriented obliquely, roughly parallel to the shaft
A key distinction is that the normal apophysis and its fragmentation lie parallel to the metatarsal, whereas an avulsion fracture line runs transversely across the bone
Pain is reproduced by resisted eversion or passive inversion that tensions the peroneus brevis
Management is conservative with activity modification, offloading and short-term immobilisation for symptom control as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Iselin disease is a traction apophysitis of the secondary ossification centre at the base of the fifth metatarsal, the site of insertion of the peroneus brevis tendon. During the period when this apophysis is developing, repetitive traction from the peroneus brevis, particularly during running, jumping and side-to-side cutting movements, stresses the cartilaginous bone-tendon junction. The repeated microtrauma causes inflammation, and the apophysis may appear enlarged or fragmented on imaging. Because the apophysis lies obliquely, roughly parallel to the long axis of the metatarsal, it can be mistaken for an avulsion fracture, which instead produces a transverse lucent line. The condition resolves once the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity.
additionalDifferentials: Avulsion fracture of the fifth metatarsal base
Jones fracture of the proximal fifth metatarsal
Peroneal tendinopathy or peroneus brevis insertional pathology
Os vesalianum (accessory ossicle at the fifth metatarsal base)
additionalInvestigations: Foot radiographs including an oblique view to assess the apophysis and exclude a fracture
Recognition of the obliquely oriented apophyseal line versus a transverse fracture line
Comparison views of the contralateral foot to gauge normal apophyseal appearance
Magnetic resonance imaging in atypical, unilateral or persistent cases
Clinical provocation with resisted eversion tensioning the peroneus brevis
Inflammatory markers if infection is suspected
redFlags: A transverse lucent line indicating an avulsion or Jones fracture rather than apophysitis
Inability to bear weight or acute severe pain after an inversion injury
Rest pain, night pain or systemic features suggesting infection or tumour
Persistent unilateral symptoms not settling with conservative treatment
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; symptoms are self-limiting and resolve as the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity, with activity modification and offloading controlling pain and no long-term sequelae expected.
pitfalls: Mistaking the normal obliquely oriented apophysis for an avulsion fracture, or vice versa
Overlooking a Jones fracture, which requires different management and has a risk of nonunion
Failing to consider infection when there is swelling, warmth or systemic upset
Prolonged immobilisation when graded activity modification would suffice
management: Relative rest and activity modification, reducing running, jumping and cutting movements until symptoms settle
Ice and simple analgesia or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain over the fifth metatarsal base
A short period of immobilisation in a stiff-soled shoe or walking boot for more severe or persistent pain
Peroneus brevis and calf stretching with a graded strengthening programme before return to sport
Reassurance that the condition is self-limiting and resolves once the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity
Gradual, symptom-guided return to activity once local tenderness has resolved
